.WHAT HAS CHANGED...

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 220 PM EDT Wednesday...

1. Showers are expected to continue this afternoon and evening 
before drier and seasonable weather returns as we head into the 
weekend.

2. Showers and thunderstorm chances increase by the end of the 
weekend with unsettled weather continuing into early next week. 
Temperatures will be relatively seasonable through the extended 
period.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 220 PM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A dying cold front is approaching northern New 
York and Vermont from Canada this afternoon, producing some 
showers out ahead of it. The forcing will decrease as it moves 
east through northern New York, but enough instability is out 
there to allow the showers to continue into Vermont. A couple 
embedded thunderstorms are possible as well. While sufficient 
deep layer shear will be in place for potentially strong storms,
low instability, some dry air aloft, a lack of well-defined 
surface boundary, and pre-existing clouds/showers will be 
working against it. Therefore, an isolated strong to severe 
storm is not likely this afternoon, but cannot be completely 
ruled out. Any storms will fall apart as they try to push 
southeast this evening and southern areas should remain mostly 
dry. Chances of lingering showers overnight are around 10-40%, 
mainly near the international border. High pressure will build 
down from Canada to end the week and start the weekend, bringing
cooler temperatures and lower humidity. Lows tonight will be 
seasonable in the 50s, then cooling late week into the 40s and 
50s. Highs through Saturday will be seasonable, with 
temperatures rising into the 70s and low 80s each afternoon. 
Next chance of precipitation arrives later Saturday afternoon 
onward.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A quasi-double barrel pattern will develop by 
late Saturday with competing pieces of energy, one over central-
eastern Ontario, and a coastal low in southern New England. 
Models depict a deepening trough over the Great Lakes by 
Saturday with a coastal low riding along the coast of southern 
New England. The deepening of the Great Lakes trough will help 
amplify our flow pattern aloft Saturday night into Sunday, 
likely accelerating the coastal low northeastward. A few showers
will be possible on the periphery of the coastal low Saturday 
night in southeastern Vermont, though majority of Vermont will 
stay dry Saturday and Saturday night. In northern New York, the 
Great Lakes trough will lead to increasing shower chances late 
Saturday into Saturday night across the St. Lawrence Valley and 
northwestern Adirondacks. Questions linger on how much moisture 
will be sandwiched between the two systems closer to Sunday 
morning, as it pertains to precipitation chances in Vermont. 
Currently there is a 35-50% chance of rain Sunday morning for 
much of Vermont, though these values may increase or decrease 
with how the trough amplification occurs. A more delayed 
amplification could keep the coastal system from racing east 
with a moisture interaction in the area between the system 
Sunday morning. A faster amplification will likely lead to less 
system interactions and perhaps a dry Sunday morning. 
Regardless, as the Great Lakes trough translates east Sunday, 
everyone will see periods of rain, and perhaps some 
thunderstorms should enough clearing take place to allow 
instability to grow. Temperatures will start off on the warmer 
than average side in the upper 70s to low 80s, though with the 
approach of clouds and showers, temperatures by Sunday will 
begin a gradual decrease back to seasonable levels.

The main piece of energy departs late Sunday, though cyclonic 
flow about a trailing upper low over eastern Ontario will keep 
some shower chances around. Lingering showers will be focused 
over the higher terrain Monday and Tuesday afternoon, mainly 
diurnally driven. Sky cover Monday and Tuesday will favor more 
clouds then sun as a result of the scattered shower chances. 
Temperatures will remain on the seasonable to potentially 
slightly below seasonable levels Monday and Tuesday with highs 
in the low to mid 70s. Temperatures will rebound by mid week 
with subtle ridging building over eastern New England.
